title: Protocols
content:
Protocols# Overview# Protocols are standardized rules and procedures that enable communication between devices over networks or serial connections. This page serves as the parent index for all protocol-related topics.
Protocol Categories# Authentication# Authentication protocols manage identity verification, access control, and centralized login for users and devices. They are widely used in enterprise networks, industrial systems, and control centers.
Common authentication protocols:
LDAP RADIUS See: Protocols/Authentication/
Data# Data protocols define the rules for exchanging operational or measurement data between devices. They are critical for industrial control, SCADA, and substation automation systems.
Common data protocols:
DNP3 Modbus IEC 61850 See: Protocols/Data/
Network# Network protocols govern device discovery, addressing, routing, and topology management. They ensure reliable and deterministic communication across local and wide-area networks.
Common network protocols:
ARP DHCP RSTP See: Protocols/Network/
Security# Security protocols provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for communications. They are essential for protecting networks, devices, and sensitive data.
Common security protocols:
IPSec SSH TLS / SSL See: Protocols/Security/

title: ARP
content:
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)# Overview# ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is a network protocol used to map layer 3 IP addresses to layer 2 MAC addresses on a local area network (LAN).
ARP operates within a broadcast domain to allow devices to determine the hardware address of a host given its IP address. It is fundamental to Ethernet communication and is used extensively in IP-based networks to enable packet delivery on local subnets.
Terminology# IP Address — logical network-layer address assigned to a host. MAC Address — hardware address assigned to a network interface card (NIC). ARP Request — broadcast message asking “Who has IP X.X.X.X?” ARP Reply — unicast response providing the MAC address for the requested IP. ARP Table / Cache — mapping of IP addresses to MAC addresses stored on a host or switch. Gratuitous ARP — ARP broadcast sent by a host to announce or update its IP-to-MAC mapping. Practical Use-Cases# Resolving MAC addresses to deliver Ethernet frames in LANs. Network troubleshooting, such as detecting IP conflicts or ARP poisoning. Switch MAC table population via ARP traffic. Network monitoring and mapping tools (e.g., identifying hosts on a subnet). Supporting VLANs and subnet communications in enterprise and industrial networks. Protocol Characteristics# Key Parameters# Transport / Layer: Operates at Layer 2 (Data Link) and assists Layer 3 (IP). Frame Type: Ethernet frame containing ARP opcode, sender/target IP/MAC addresses. Message Types: Request, Reply, Gratuitous. Cache Timeout: ARP table entries expire after a configurable period (commonly 60–120 seconds). Broadcast Domain: ARP requests are broadcast to all devices on the same subnet. Best Practices# Minimize unnecessary ARP broadcasts in large networks using static ARP entries or ARP caching. Monitor ARP traffic for anomalies or potential attacks. Use VLAN segmentation to limit ARP broadcast domains. Combine with security features like Dynamic ARP Inspection (on managed switches) to prevent spoofing. Clear stale ARP cache entries on network devices as needed. Common Pitfalls# ARP cache poisoning / spoofing causing network attacks or misrouting. Excessive ARP traffic in large broadcast domains leading to congestion. Stale ARP entries preventing communication after device replacement or MAC change. Misconfigured subnet masks causing ARP requests to fail. Gratuitous ARP flooding in misconfigured networks. ARP Message Flow Overview# Message Type Description ARP Request Broadcast sent to ask “Who has IP X.X.X.X?” ARP Reply Unicast response with the MAC address corresponding to the requested IP. Gratuitous ARP Broadcast to announce a host’s IP/MAC mapping, typically used at startup or after IP changes. Troubleshooting & Failure Modes# Symptoms# Hosts cannot reach other hosts on the same subnet. Duplicate IP address warnings. Intermittent connectivity within LAN. Unexpected traffic rerouting or interception (potential ARP spoofing). ARP table inconsistencies or missing entries. Root Causes# Incorrect IP or subnet configuration. MAC address changes not reflected in ARP cache. Malicious ARP spoofing or poisoning. Network loops or broadcast storms. Device misconfiguration or failed interface. Fixes / Workarounds# Clear or refresh ARP cache (arp -d or OS-specific commands). Verify IP addressing and subnet mask configurations. Use static ARP entries for critical devices if necessary. Deploy security features like Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI). Monitor ARP traffic for anomalies using network analysis tools. Field Test Methods# arp -a to view ARP cache on hosts. Ping and trace to test MAC resolution and reachability. Packet capture with Wireshark or tcpdump to inspect ARP requests and replies. Network mapping tools to identify IP/MAC pairings. Test duplicate IP detection and conflict resolution. Standards & References# RFC 826 — ARP protocol specification. IEEE 802.3 — Ethernet framing and addressing standards. RFC 5227 — IPv4 Address Conflict Detection. Cisco / vendor documentation — ARP security and monitoring practices.

title: BNC
content:
BNC Coaxial Port# Overview# The BNC (Bayonet Neill–Concelman) connector is a quick-connect, bayonet-style RF connector used for coaxial cabling. It is widely used in instrumentation, oscilloscopes, radios, lab equipment, GPS timing receivers, and video systems.
Terminology# BNC — Bayonet-style RF connector for coaxial cable. Coax — Cable with center conductor, dielectric, shielding, and outer jacket. 50 Ω / 75 Ω — Characteristic impedance types; matching required for proper signal integrity. RG-58 / RG-59 / RG-6 — Common coax cable types. IRIG-B — Time synchronization signal used in power systems and industrial automation. Return Loss — Reflection due to impedance mismatch. TDR — Time-Domain Reflectometry used for cable diagnostics. Practical Use-Cases# Oscilloscope and signal analyzer inputs/outputs GPS-disciplined clocks and timing distribution IRIG-B time code distribution (power systems, substations, PMUs) Function generator outputs RF equipment and receivers CCTV and SDI video systems Legacy 10BASE2 networking (historical) Configuration & Implementation# Key Parameters# Impedance: 50 Ω for RF, instrumentation, IRIG-B 75 Ω for video (CCTV, SDI) Frequency range: up to ~4 GHz depending on connector grade Cable types: RG-58 (50 Ω) RG-59/6 (75 Ω) Termination: 50 Ω or 75 Ω termination resistors depending on system Connection style: Bayonet twist-lock; plug ↔ jack Best Practices# Always match connector and cable impedance (50 Ω or 75 Ω). Keep coax runs short when transporting high-frequency or timing signals. Avoid sharp bends that deform the dielectric. Label coax cables when distributing IRIG-B around a substation. Use strain relief on portable test equipment. Avoid adapters (BNC-to-SMA, etc.) unless absolutely necessary. Common Pitfalls# Using 75 Ω BNC on 50 Ω timing equipment. Running IRIG-B through patch panels or couplers that distort the waveform. Long coax runs causing amplitude droop (especially for AM IRIG-B). Damaged or loose bayonet connectors leading to intermittent signals. Water ingress in outdoor coax. Using low-frequency coax for RF applications. Typical Protocols / Signals# BNC connectors are used to carry:
Analog RF signals Oscilloscope probe signals Clock/trigger outputs Composite video SDI (Serial Digital Interface) GPS reference outputs (1 PPS, 10 MHz) IRIG-B time synchronization signals (AM or DC) Low-frequency RF Substation timing distribution Troubleshooting & Failure Modes# Symptoms# No signal or missing sync Excessive noise or distortion Bad video or timing errors PMU desynchronization Oscilloscope ringing on square pulses Intermittent triggers Root Causes# Impedance mismatch (50 Ω ↔ 75 Ω) Damaged coax or crushed dielectric Missing termination on IRIG-B or video links Water or corrosion Cable too long for the frequency/timing signal Loose or worn bayonet connectors Fixes / Workarounds# Replace damaged coax Add or verify correct termination Ensure impedance is matched end-to-end Use high-quality RG-58 for IRIG-B Avoid T-connectors unless required by legacy systems Clean or replace corroded connectors Field Test Methods# Continuity testers TDR for impedance & distance-to-fault Oscilloscope for IRIG-B waveform verification Spectrum analyzer or VNA for RF SDI monitors for video integrity SEL/Arbiter clock status screens Standards & References# IEC 60169-8 — BNC connector standard IRIG Standard 200-04 / 200-16 — IRIG time code formats IEEE C37.118 — Synchrophasor & timing requirements SMPTE 259M / 292M / 424M — SDI coax video standards IEEE 802.3 (10BASE2) — Historical coax Ethernet

title: DB25
content:
DB25 Serial Connector# Overview# The DB25 is a 25-pin D-subminiature connector historically used for RS-232 serial communication, parallel interfaces, and other legacy protocols. While largely replaced by DB9 for modern serial ports, DB25 remains in use for industrial devices, protection relays, and legacy equipment requiring full handshake control or multiple serial lines.
DB25 connectors carry asynchronous serial signals, supporting point-to-point communication over longer cable lengths when properly wired.
Terminology# DB25 — D-sub connector with 25 pins. RS-232 / RS-422 / RS-485 — serial communication standards using DB25. DTE / DCE — Data Terminal Equipment / Data Communication Equipment; determines pinout orientation. Null Modem — cable wiring variant that crosses Tx/Rx and handshake signals for DTE↔DTE connections. Baud rate — communication speed (e.g., 9600, 19200, 115200 bps). Parity / Stop Bits / Data Bits — serial framing configuration. Full handshaking — DB25 provides additional control lines (e.g., 8 handshake signals) compared to DB9. Practical Use-Cases# Relay, IED, or PLC engineering access ports. Industrial automation device connections requiring full hardware handshaking. SCADA and substation communication links. Lab equipment and test instrumentation. Legacy RS-232 serial consoles and multi-line communication. Electrical & Signal Characteristics# Key Parameters# Voltage levels: ±3 to ±15 V for RS-232 signaling Max cable length: ~15 m (50 ft) typical, depending on baud rate and environment Signal lines: Data: TxD, RxD Ground: GND Handshake: RTS, CTS, DTR, DSR, DCD, RI, optional secondary lines Communication: asynchronous, full-duplex, point-to-point Baud rate support: device-dependent, typically up to 115200 bps Best Practices# Use proper shielded serial cables in electrically noisy environments. Match DTE/DCE orientation or use null modem cables if connecting DTE↔DTE. Keep cable lengths within RS-232 limits. Terminate unused handshake lines according to device requirements. Label cables for Tx/Rx and handshake lines to prevent miswiring. Common Pitfalls# Miswiring Tx/Rx or handshake signals. Baud rate or framing mismatch between devices. Exceeding cable length limits causing errors. Electrical noise or ground loops. Bent pins or connector damage, especially with repeated insertion/removal. Pinout# Standard DB25 (RS-232 DTE) pinout:
Pin Signal Description 1 GND Signal Ground 2 TxD Transmit Data 3 RxD Receive Data 4 RTS Request to Send 5 CTS Clear to Send 6 DSR Data Set Ready 7 GND Signal Ground 8 DCD Data Carrier Detect 9 +V Optional +V supply 10 -V Optional -V supply 11 Unassigned / Secondary handshake … … … … (pins 12–25 vary by device, often unassigned) Note: DB25 pinout varies widely for different DTE/DCE devices. Always verify device documentation before connecting.
Configuration Considerations# Baud rate / data format: must match between devices. Handshake lines: DB25 supports full hardware handshaking. Cable type: straight-through for DTE↔DCE, null modem for DTE↔DTE. Termination: some devices require pull-ups/pull-downs for unused control lines. Troubleshooting & Failure Modes# Symptoms# No data received or transmitted. Garbled or intermittent data. Handshake or flow-control errors. Device not recognized or fails to initialize. Root Causes# Miswiring Tx/Rx or handshake lines. Incorrect baud rate, parity, stop bits, or data bits. Broken cable, bent pins, or connector damage. Electrical noise or ground loops. Flow control not properly configured. Fixes / Workarounds# Verify and correct wiring or use null modem cables. Match serial port settings exactly (baud, parity, stop, data bits). Replace damaged cables or connectors. Use shielded cables and ferrites in noisy environments. Perform loopback testing to isolate faults. Field Test Methods# Serial loopback test (short Tx↔Rx) Cable continuity tester for DB25 pins Oscilloscope or logic analyzer to view signals Software-based port diagnostics Visual inspection for bent pins Standards & References# EIA/TIA-232 — RS-232 standard for serial communication. RS-422 / RS-485 — differential serial standards sometimes using DB25. IEC 61158 / IEC 61850 — substation serial communication applications. TIA-568 — structured cabling references where applicable.

title: DB9
content:
DB9 Serial Connector# Overview# The DB9 is a 9-pin D-subminiature connector commonly used for RS-232 serial communication. It is widely found on legacy equipment, industrial devices, protection relays, PLCs, and configuration ports.
DB9 connectors carry asynchronous serial signals, supporting point-to-point communication over relatively short distances. Some devices also use them for console or control interfaces.
Terminology# DB9 — D-sub connector with 9 pins. RS-232 / RS-422 / RS-485 — serial communication standards that may use DB9. DTE / DCE — Data Terminal Equipment / Data Communication Equipment; determines pinout orientation. Null Modem — a cable wiring variant that crosses Tx/Rx signals for direct device-to-device connection. Baud rate — communication speed (e.g., 9600, 19200, 115200 bps). Parity / Stop Bits / Data Bits — serial framing configuration. Practical Use-Cases# Relay or IED configuration and monitoring. Industrial automation device connections. SCADA or substation engineering access. Legacy console ports on networking or server equipment. Lab equipment and test devices. Electrical & Signal Characteristics# Key Parameters# Voltage levels: ±3 to ±15 V for RS-232 signaling Max cable length: ~15 m (50 ft) typical, depending on baud rate Signal lines: Tx, Rx, GND, optional handshake lines (RTS, CTS, DTR, DSR, DCD, RI) Communication: asynchronous, full-duplex, point-to-point Baud rate support: device-dependent, typically up to 115200 bps Best Practices# Use proper shielded serial cables in electrically noisy environments. Match DTE/DCE orientation or use a null modem if needed. Keep cable lengths within RS-232 limits to avoid signal degradation. Terminate unused handshake lines appropriately. Label cables for Tx/Rx direction clarity. Common Pitfalls# Miswiring Tx/Rx signals causing no communication. Baud rate or framing mismatch between devices. Excessive cable length leading to errors. Ground loops or noise introducing data corruption. Damaged pins or bent connectors. Pinout# Standard DB9 (RS-232 DTE) pinout:
Pin Signal Description 1 DCD Data Carrier Detect 2 RxD Receive Data 3 TxD Transmit Data 4 DTR Data Terminal Ready 5 GND Signal Ground 6 DSR Data Set Ready 7 RTS Request to Send 8 CTS Clear to Send 9 RI Ring Indicator Note: Pinouts vary for DCE devices or null modem cables.
Configuration Considerations# Baud rate / data format: must match between devices. Handshake lines: optional RTS/CTS or XON/XOFF software flow control. Cable type: straight-through for DTE↔DCE, crossover for DTE↔DTE. Termination: unused lines may require pull-ups/pull-downs in some industrial equipment. Troubleshooting & Failure Modes# Symptoms# No data received or transmitted. Garbled or intermittent data. Flow-control handshake errors. Device not recognized or fails to initialize. Root Causes# Tx/Rx miswiring or DTE/DCE mismatch. Incorrect baud rate, parity, stop bits, or data bits. Broken cable, bent pins, or loose connectors. Electrical noise or ground loop interference. Flow control lines not properly configured. Fixes / Workarounds# Verify and correct wiring or use null modem cable. Match serial port settings exactly (baud, parity, stop, data bits). Replace damaged cables or connectors. Use shielded cables or ferrites in noisy environments. Test with loopback adapters to isolate faults. Field Test Methods# Serial loopback test (short Rx↔Tx) Cable continuity tester for DB9 pins Oscilloscope or logic analyzer to view signal waveform Software-based port diagnostics and data logging Standards & References# EIA/TIA-232 — RS-232 standard for serial communication. RS-422 / RS-485 — differential serial standards sometimes using DB9. IEC 61158 / IEC 61850 — for serial links in substation automation (application-specific). TIA-568 — structured cabling references for serial interfaces where applicable.

title: DHCP
content:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)# Overview# DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is a network protocol that automatically assigns IP addresses and other network configuration parameters to devices on a network.
DHCP simplifies IP address management, ensures proper subnet configuration, and supports centralized management of network parameters such as default gateway, DNS servers, and lease times. It is widely used in enterprise networks, industrial LANs, and service provider networks.
Terminology# DHCP Client — device requesting IP configuration (e.g., PC, IoT device, relay). DHCP Server — authoritative device providing IP addresses and configuration. IP Lease — temporary allocation of an IP address to a client. DHCP Scope / Pool — defined range of IP addresses available for assignment. DHCP Discover / Offer / Request / Ack — primary message types in the DHCP handshake. DHCP NACK — message indicating a requested IP cannot be assigned. DHCP Relay / Agent — intermediary forwarding DHCP messages between clients and servers across subnets. Option / Parameter — additional network settings delivered by DHCP (e.g., DNS, gateway, domain name). Practical Use-Cases# Automatic IP assignment for client devices in enterprise networks. Configuration of SCADA, PLCs, and industrial devices without manual IP setup. Simplified network management in large campus networks. Temporary or dynamic IP allocation in service provider or cloud networks. Support for mobile devices and wireless networks. Protocol Characteristics# Key Parameters# Ports: UDP 67 (server), UDP 68 (client) Transport: UDP (connectionless, requires broadcast for initial discovery) Message Types: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack, NACK, Release, Inform Lease Duration: Configurable per scope; determines how long a client may use an IP. Options: Network configuration parameters including gateway, DNS, subnet mask, domain name, TFTP server, etc. Best Practices# Segment DHCP scopes per subnet or VLAN to avoid IP conflicts. Use DHCP reservations for critical devices (relays, servers, routers). Configure redundant DHCP servers for high availability. Monitor lease usage and enforce appropriate lease times. Secure DHCP with trusted relay agents and optional authentication in sensitive environments. Common Pitfalls# IP exhaustion due to undersized scope or rogue clients. Duplicate IP addresses from misconfigured static assignments. Misconfigured DHCP relay or firewall blocking DHCP traffic. DHCP server misconfiguration causing clients to fail obtaining IP addresses. Broadcast domain issues preventing DHCP discover messages from reaching the server. DHCP Message Flow Overview# Message Type Description DHCP Discover Client broadcasts to locate available DHCP servers. DHCP Offer Server responds with an available IP address and network parameters. DHCP Request Client requests the offered IP address from a specific server. DHCP Ack Server confirms assignment and provides full configuration. DHCP NACK Server denies the requested IP assignment. DHCP Release Client releases the IP address back to the pool. DHCP Inform Client requests additional configuration parameters without changing IP. Troubleshooting & Failure Modes# Symptoms# Clients cannot obtain IP addresses. IP conflicts or duplicate addresses on the network. Incorrect gateway, DNS, or subnet mask configuration. Intermittent connectivity due to lease expiration or renewal issues. DHCP offers not reaching clients across subnets. Root Causes# DHCP server down or unreachable. Broadcast traffic blocked by firewalls or VLAN segmentation. Exhausted DHCP scope or pool. Misconfigured relay agents or IP helper addresses. Incorrect DHCP options (gateway, DNS) configured on server. Fixes / Workarounds# Verify DHCP server is running and accessible. Ensure UDP ports 67/68 are open and allowed across the network. Expand DHCP scope or reclaim unused leases. Configure relay agents correctly for multi-subnet networks. Validate DHCP options for proper network configuration. Field Test Methods# ipconfig /renew (Windows) or dhclient (Linux) to test client lease assignment. Capture DHCP packets with Wireshark or tcpdump to inspect Discover/Offer/Request/Ack flow. Monitor DHCP server logs for errors or lease utilization. Test relay agent functionality in multi-subnet environments. Check IP conflicts and lease expiration behavior. Standards & References# RFC 2131 — DHCP Protocol Specification. RFC 2132 — DHCP Options and Parameters. RFC 1542 — BootP Relay and related considerations. IETF DHCP Working Group — updates, best practices, and extensions.
